questions.question: Why does adding a reason to an instruction usually improve results?
options: It makes the prompt longer, which models prefer
The model can apply the spirit of the rule to cases you did not list
Reasons are required by the API
It reduces the number of tokens in the output
questions.explanation: Explaining the purpose lets the model generalise the rule sensibly instead of applying it only to the literal cases mentioned.

questions.question: Which is the best rewrite of "Don't make it too technical"?
options: DO NOT BE TECHNICAL UNDER ANY CIRCUMSTANCES
Avoid technical words, jargon, terms and acronyms
Make it non-technical and not too complex
Explain it as you would to a branch manager with no IT background
questions.explanation: Positive, specific instructions describe the desired behaviour and audience rather than only what to avoid.

questions.question: What is the typical effect of shouty prompts such as "CRITICAL!!! YOU MUST ALWAYS..." on current models?
options: Over-application: the rule is applied rigidly even where it no longer makes sense
The model ignores the instruction entirely
The model becomes more accurate at arithmetic
No effect at all, since models ignore capital letters
questions.explanation: Modern models already follow instructions closely, so aggressive emphasis tends to make them over-apply the rule; calm, explained wording works better.

questions.question: A prompt says both "Be concise" and "Cover every clause in detail". What should you do?
options: Leave both; the model will balance them
Put one of them in capital letters
Decide which goal wins, or explain how both apply, and state it clearly
questions.explanation: Contradictions force the model to guess which instruction to obey; resolving them explicitly makes behaviour predictable.
